Theme

Time, the calendar & feasts

ancient adjective

also the ancients, in ancient times, age-old, of old, olden, in antiquity

classical

Cic. Leg. 1.55: quod decus antīquī summum bonum esse dīxērunt (Lewis & Short)
Liv. 39.6.9: vīlissimum antīquīs mancipium

antīquus, antīqua, antīquum

adjective · Declension on Wiktionary

ancient, of former times

What belongs to a time long past, the opposite of novus; as a noun, antīquī are the ancients, above all the old writers. It can also mean simply former, earlier, and its comparative, more important: quod honestius, id mihi est antīquius (Cic. Att. 7.3, Lewis & Short). For a worn object say vetus (see old).

Other words

  • vetus, veteris — old, of long standing; as a noun, the men of old

    adjective, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Univ. 11: crēdendum est veteribus et prīscīs virīs (Lewis & Short, s.v. prīscus)

    Lewis & Short sets the two apart: vetus is what has existed a long time (the opposite of recēns), antīquus what belongs to a time that is past. Veterēs, too, are the ancients.

  • prīscus, prīsca, prīscum — of olden times, ancient, venerable

    adjective · also used · classical · Hor. Epod. 2.2: ut prīsca gēns mortālium; Ov. Ars 3.121; de Vaan 489 · Declension on Wiktionary

    What was there before our time, with a sense of venerable age; from Augustus on, what dates from the earliest days of Rome (Lewis & Short). Lewis & Short leaves the i unmarked; de Vaan prints prīscus, and the loci write prīsca.

  • antīquitus — in former times, of old

    adverb · also used · classical · Caes. BG 2.4: Belgās Rhēnum antīquitus trāductōs (Lewis & Short s.v. antīquus); Traupman 271

    Not in Cicero (Lewis & Short); chiefly in the historians.

Examples

  • tum coquus, vīlissimum antīquīs mancipium et aestimātiōne et ūsū, in pretiō esse, et quod ministerium fuerat, ars habērī coepta

    then the cook, to the ancients the cheapest of slaves both in value and in use, began to be prized, and what had been a chore came to be thought an artLiv. 39.6.9

  • Oblīviōnis antīquīs dictus multumque fābulōsus

    (the river Limia,) called the river of Forgetfulness by the ancients, and the stuff of many talesPlin. NH 4.115

  • prīsca juvent aliōs: ego mē nunc dēnique nātum grātulor: haec aetās mōribus apta meīs

    let the old days please others: I am glad I was born now; this age suits my waysOv. Ars 3.121–122

  • sērō tē amāvī, pulchritūdō tam antīqua et tam nova

    late have I loved you, beauty so ancient and so newAug. Conf. 10.27.38

See also old, modern, traditional, history.
